title: US Unveils Economic D-Day Sanctions Against Iran as Tehran Threatens Gulf Oil Shutdown
excerpt: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announces what he calls the greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary, while Iran warns it will halt all oil exports from the Persian Gulf.
body:
• The US is rolling out sweeping new sanctions against Iran on Monday, targeting countries and entities that maintain economic ties with Tehran.
  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called it "the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary" in a Financial Times op-ed.
  • Iran has threatened to shut down all oil exports from the Persian Gulf if the economic pressure continues, calling the sanctions "an act of war."
  • China, which purchases over 80% of Iran's shipped oil, has urged diplomacy, saying "sanctions and pressure do not help resolve the problem."

Washington Escalates Economic Warfare

The United States is set to impose what it describes as the most aggressive financial sanctions package in history against Iran, marking a decisive shift in strategy as the six-month-old conflict enters a new phase of economic confrontation.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will hold a press conference at 2 p.m. EDT on Monday to detail the measures, following days of escalating rhetoric from Washington. In an opinion piece published in the Financial Times on Sunday, Bessent framed the move in stark military terms.

"At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary," Bessent wrote, signaling that the US would target nations engaging in "appeasement" by maintaining economic ties with Iran.

Iran's Defiant Response

Tehran has responded with threats of its own. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, warned Sunday that the consequences would extend far beyond Iran's borders.

"If the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported, neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf. Iran will regard any country's participation in or support for America's economic war against the Iranian people as an act of war."

— Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council

Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi earlier dismissed the strategy as a distraction from America's domestic economic challenges. "The so-called 'Economic D-Day' is a diversion from America's own crisis: unprecedented debt and surging interest costs," Araghchi said on social media.

Iran's Armed Forces Chief of Staff, Major General Ali Abdollahi, went further, promising "crushing, punishing and devastating responses" across "land, sea, air, air defence and cyberspace."

A Strategic Pivot From Military to Economic Pressure

The sanctions escalation represents a tactical shift by Washington. The US and Israel launched military strikes against Iran beginning February 28, killing thousands including Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and degrading much of Iran's conventional military capacity.

But Iran has preserved enough missile and drone capability to threaten oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, bringing shipping in the key waterway to a near standstill and pressuring global fuel prices. Two ceasefire deals — in April and June — both collapsed quickly.

Bessent suggested the economic approach could reduce the need for further military action. "If we are doing the maximum economic pressure, then that means that likely there will not be a large-scale kinetic restart," he told CNBC last week.

China Factor Looms Large

The sanctions put China in a difficult position. Beijing purchases more than 80% of Iran's shipped oil, according to 2025 data from analytics firm Kpler. A spokesperson for China's embassy in Washington responded cautiously, stating that "sanctions and pressure do not help resolve the problem" while calling for diplomatic solutions.

Oil prices rose to more than a three-week high following the initial sanctions threats, though Bessent argued markets were misreading the situation. "I'm not sure why oil has popped up on this," he told CNBC.

What Comes Next

Without detailed specifics ahead of Monday's announcement, Bessent has signaled the measures will target "fearful nations" that continue doing business with Iran. The UAE has already suspended financial and economic transactions with Tehran.

Pakistan's army chief, Asim Munir, is expected to visit Tehran on Monday as part of ongoing mediation efforts, though the warring nations have not engaged in face-to-face talks since June negotiations in Switzerland.

Iran entered the conflict already burdened by high inflation, a weakening currency, energy shortages, and decades of sanctions. The new measures threaten to compound those pressures at a time when the country must also contend with damaged infrastructure and disrupted trade from months of military strikes.
